triples.relationship: childbirth associated with a people's restoration
triples.rationale: Micah connects the woman's giving birth with the remaining brothers' return to Israel. Isaiah connects Zion giving birth to her children with the birth of a nation. The shared childbirth-and-people imagery does not identify Micah's unnamed woman with a particular individual.
triples.source_text: Therefore he will give them up until the time of the woman giving birth, when she gives birth; then the remaining ones of their brothers will return to the sons of Israel.

target_units.text: Before the woman in labor gave birth, before the pain of labor came, she escaped and bore a male.
Who heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? Did a land labor in one day, or was a nation born all at once? For Zion labored and bore her children.
‘But I gave this expectation, and you did not remember Me,’ said the Lord. ‘Behold, did I not make the woman who gives birth and the barren woman?’ said God.

triples.relationship: parallel shepherd-ruler promises
triples.rationale: Micah's promised ruler will shepherd his flock in the Lord's strength. Ezekiel likewise promises one shepherd, God's servant David, and calls him a ruler among the people, joining shepherding with rule under the Lord.
triples.source_text: He will stand, see and shepherd his flock in the Lord’s strength, and they will exist in the glory of the name of the Lord their God; for now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth.

target_units.text: I will raise up one shepherd over them, My servant David, and he will shepherd them and be their shepherd.
I, the Lord, will be their God, and David a ruler among them. I, the Lord, have spoken.

triples.relationship: parallel response to Assyrian intrusion
triples.rationale: Micah describes an Assyrian entering the land and a response raised against him. Isaiah promises destruction of the Assyrians from the Lord's land and mountains. Both address Assyrian intrusion and its reversal; Micah's seven shepherds and eight bites wording is left intact.
triples.source_text: This will be peace: when an Assyrian comes upon your land and steps upon your country, seven shepherds and eight bites of people will rise against him.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “As I said, so it will be, and as I counseled, so it will endure,
to destroy the Assyrians from My land and from My mountains. They will become a trampling place; their yoke will be removed from them, and their glory removed from the shoulders.”

triples.relationship: parallel deliverance from Assyria's power
triples.rationale: Micah promises rescue from Assour when he crosses the land's borders. Isaiah similarly announces removal of the Assyrians from the land and removal of their yoke from shoulders.
triples.source_text: They will shepherd Assour with the sword and Nebrod’s land in its ditch. He will rescue from Assour when he comes upon your land and steps upon your borders.

target_units.text: to destroy the Assyrians from My land and from My mountains. They will become a trampling place; their yoke will be removed from them, and their glory removed from the shoulders.”

triples.relationship: dew imagery connected with Israel and the Lord
triples.rationale: Micah compares Jacob's remnant among the peoples with dew falling from the Lord. Hosea promises that the Lord will be like dew to Israel. Both connect Israel and dew with the Lord, while assigning the image differently.
triples.source_text: Jacob’s remnant will be among the nations, amid many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord and like lambs upon couch grass, so that no one may be gathered or stand among the sons of humankind.

target_units.text: I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.

triples.relationship: shared lion imagery with no rescuer
triples.rationale: Micah depicts the remnant as a lion seizing among flocks with no one to deliver. Hosea likewise uses a lion comparison and seizure with no one to rescue. Micah applies the image to the remnant; Hosea applies it to the Lord's judgment against Judah.
triples.source_text: Jacob’s remnant will be among the nations, amid many peoples, like a lion among beasts in the forest and like a young lion among flocks of sheep, which passes through, separates and seizes, with no one to deliver.

target_units.text: For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to Judah’s house. I seize and will go away and take, and there will be no one to rescue.

triples.relationship: hands over enemies as victory imagery
triples.rationale: Micah promises the hand raised over afflicting enemies. Jacob's blessing of Judah likewise places his hands upon his enemies' backs, using the position of the hand to express victory over opponents.
triples.source_text: Your hand will be raised above those afflicting you, and all your enemies will be destroyed.

target_units.text: “Judah, may your brothers praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies, and your father’s sons shall bow down to you.

triples.relationship: parallel removal of horses and chariots
triples.rationale: Micah announces destruction of the people's horses and chariots. Zechariah likewise announces the destruction of chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, placing that removal beside peace and the coming king's rule.
triples.source_text: “On that day,” says the Lord, “I will destroy your horses from your midst and destroy your chariots,

target_units.text: He will destroy chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; the battle bow will be destroyed, and abundance and peace from the nations. He will rule waters as far as the sea and the earth’s river outlets.

triples.relationship: judgment on fortified cities
triples.rationale: Micah promises to destroy cities and remove strongholds. Hosea specifically condemns Judah's multiplication of walled cities and announces fire that will devour their foundations.
triples.source_text: and I will destroy the cities of your land and remove all your strongholds.

target_units.text: Israel forgot his Maker, and they built sacred precincts; Judah multiplied walled cities. I will send fire into his cities, and it will devour their foundations.

triples.relationship: removal of forbidden sorcery and divination
triples.rationale: Micah announces removal of sorceries and utterers of oracles. Deuteronomy forbids sorcery, divination and related practices among Israel and contrasts the nations' reliance on them with the Lord's instruction.
triples.source_text: I will remove your sorceries from your hands, and there will be no utterers of oracles among you.

target_units.text: There shall not be found among you one who purifies his son or his daughter by fire, or practises divination, or interprets spoken omens, or observes auguries, or works sorcery,
or chants spells, or is a medium, or observes portents, or inquires of the dead.
For everyone who does these things is an abomination unto the Lord your God; for because of these abominations the Lord shall destroy them from before you.
You shall be perfect before the Lord your God.
For these nations whose possession you inherit hearken unto omens and divinations; but the Lord your God has not granted you so to do.

triples.relationship: parallel destruction of images and pillars
triples.rationale: Micah promises destruction of carved images and pillars and an end to bowing to handmade works. Deuteronomy commands the breaking of pillars and burning of graven images, sharing the elimination of these objects of worship.
triples.source_text: I will destroy your carved images and pillars from your midst, and you will certainly no longer bow down to the works of your hands.

target_units.text: And you shall pull down their altars, and break their pillars, and cut down their sacred groves, and burn the graven images of their gods with fire; and their name shall perish from that place.

triples.relationship: parallel cutting down of sacred groves
triples.rationale: Micah promises to cut down the groves from the people's midst. Deuteronomy specifically commands cutting down sacred groves along with destroying other objects of foreign worship.
triples.source_text: I will cut down your groves from your midst and obliterate your cities.

target_units.text: And you shall pull down their altars, and break their pillars, and cut down their sacred groves, and burn the graven images of their gods with fire; and their name shall perish from that place.

triples.relationship: parallel wrath against nations
triples.rationale: Micah announces vengeance in anger and wrath among disobedient nations. Isaiah summons nations to hear that the Lord's wrath and anger are against them for destruction, matching the announced agent, recipients and punitive anger.
triples.source_text: I will execute vengeance in anger and wrath among the nations because they did not obey.”

target_units.text: Draw near, nations, and hear, rulers! Let the earth and those in it hear, the inhabited world and the people in it!
For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.

triples.relationship: creation summoned to hear the divine case
triples.rationale: Micah calls for the mountains and hills to hear the word in the setting of judgment. Moses likewise calls heaven and earth to hear his words, using creation as the audience to a declaration concerning God and His people.
triples.source_text: Hear now the word of the Lord. The Lord said: “Rise, enter into judgment before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.”

target_units.text: Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

triples.relationship: creation as witness to God's judgment of His people
triples.rationale: Micah calls the hills, ravines and earth's foundations to hear the Lord's case with Israel. The psalm likewise summons heaven and earth to God's judgment of His covenant people and declares God the judge.
triples.source_text: Hear, hills, the Lord’s judgment, and you ravines, foundations of the earth! For the Lord has a case against His people, and He will argue it with Israel.

target_units.text: He will summon heaven above and the earth, to judge His people.
Gather His holy ones to Him, those who establish His covenant over sacrifices.
The heavens will announce His righteousness, for God is judge. Diapsalma.

triples.relationship: parallel divine question about an alleged offense
triples.rationale: The Lord asks His people what He has done to grieve or trouble them. Jeremiah similarly asks what offense their fathers found in Him that led them away, framing the people's departure against God's challenge to name His wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: “My people, what have I done to you? How have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer Me!

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: What offense did your fathers find in Me, that they withdrew far from Me, followed futile things and became futile?

triples.relationship: explicit recollection of deliverance from slavery
triples.rationale: Micah recalls the Lord bringing Israel from Egypt and redeeming them from the house of slavery. Exodus uses that same Egypt-and-house-of-bondage description in the Lord's declaration introducing the commandments.
triples.source_text: For I brought you up from Egypt’s land and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam before you.

target_units.text: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

triples.relationship: explicit recollection of Balak and Balaam
triples.rationale: Micah commands remembrance of Balak's plan and Balaam's answer. Numbers records Balak summoning Balaam to curse Jacob, Balaam's refusal to curse those God does not curse, and Balak's complaint that a blessing was given instead.
triples.source_text: My people, remember what Balak king of Moab planned against you and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from the rushes to Galgal, so that the Lord’s righteousness may be known.”

target_units.text: And God's Spirit came upon him, and he took up his parable and said: Balak summoned me from Mesopotamia, the king of Moab from the eastern mountains: Come, curse Jacob for me; come, call down a curse on Israel for me.
Why should I curse whom the Lord does not curse? Why should I call down a curse on whom God does not curse?
From the tops of mountains I shall see them, and from the hills I shall observe them. Behold, a people who will dwell alone, not counted among the nations.
Who has measured Jacob’s seed exactly, and who will count Israel's clans? May my soul die among righteous souls, and may my seed be like their seed!
And Balak said to Balaam: What have you done to me? I summoned you to curse my enemies, and look, you have pronounced a blessing!
And Balaam said to Balak: Must I not take care to speak what God puts in my mouth?

triples.relationship: questioning the sufficiency of animal offerings
triples.rationale: Micah asks whether burnt offerings and calves can secure approach to God. The psalm likewise discusses continual burnt offerings, refuses calves and questions whether God eats bulls' flesh, directing attention beyond merely supplying sacrificial animals.
triples.source_text: With what shall I take hold of the Lord and grasp my God Most High? Shall I take hold of Him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves?

target_units.text: I will not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before Me.
I will not receive calves from your house or young goats from your flocks.
For all the forest’s wild animals are Mine, beasts on the mountains and cattle.
I know all the birds of heaven, and the field’s beauty is with Me.
If I become hungry, I will certainly not tell you, for the inhabited world and its fullness are Mine.
Will I eat bulls’ flesh or drink goats’ blood?

triples.relationship: sacrificial abundance contrasted with obedience
triples.rationale: Micah asks whether thousands of rams can satisfy the Lord before stating what He seeks in the next verse. Samuel explicitly places listening and obedience above sacrifice and the fat of rams.
triples.source_text: Will the Lord receive with thousands of rams or with ten thousands of fat-rich torrents? Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties, the fruit of my body for the sin of my life?

target_units.text: Samuel said, “Are whole burnt offerings and sacrifices as desirable to the Lord as listening to the Lord’s voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness than the fat of rams.

triples.relationship: firstborn sacrifice considered against the rejection of child offerings
triples.rationale: Micah asks whether a firstborn child could be given for sin, followed by the Lord's ethical requirements. Deuteronomy explicitly rejects the nations' burning of sons and daughters as practices the Lord hates, bearing on the proposed child offering.
triples.source_text: Will the Lord receive with thousands of rams or with ten thousands of fat-rich torrents? Shall I give my firstborn offspring for impieties, the fruit of my body for the sin of my life?

target_units.text: You shall not do so unto the Lord your God; for the abominations which the Lord hated they did unto their gods, for they burn their sons and their daughters with fire unto their gods.

triples.relationship: parallel statement of what the Lord requires
triples.rationale: Micah asks what the Lord seeks and names justice, mercy and readiness to walk with Him. Deuteronomy likewise asks what He requires and names fear, walking in His ways, love, service and keeping His commands.
triples.source_text: Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

target_units.text: And now, O Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul,
to keep the commandments of the Lord your God, and His ordinances which I command you this day, that it may be well with you?

triples.relationship: justice and mercy as weighty requirements
triples.rationale: Micah identifies doing justice and loving mercy among what God seeks. Jesus likewise names justice and mercy among the Law's weightier matters, contrasting their neglect with meticulous tithing.
triples.source_text: Has it been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord seek from you, except to do justice, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

target_units.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, but have left aside the weightier matters of the Law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness! These you ought to have done without leaving those aside.

triples.relationship: salvation promised to those who fear the Lord
triples.rationale: Micah says the Lord will save those who fear His name. The psalm likewise says He hears and saves those who fear Him, directly joining reverence and rescue.
triples.source_text: The Lord’s voice will be called to the city, and He will save those who fear His name. “Hear, tribe! And who will adorn a city?

target_units.text: He will fulfill the will of those who fear Him; He will hear their plea and save them.

triples.relationship: treasure and the lawless person
triples.rationale: Micah exposes a lawless person's house storing lawless treasures. Proverbs warns that treasures do not profit lawless people and contrasts them with righteousness that rescues from death.
triples.source_text: Is there not fire, and a lawless person’s house storing lawless treasures, and injustice with insolence?

target_units.text: Treasures will not profit lawless people, but righteousness will rescue from death.

triples.relationship: deceptive weights opposed to the legal standard
triples.rationale: Micah questions whether a lawless person can be justified with deceptive weights in a pouch. Deuteronomy expressly forbids differing weights in the pouch, requires just weights and condemns the injustice.
triples.source_text: Will a lawless person be justified with a balance and deceptive weights in a pouch?

target_units.text: You shall not have in your pouch differing weights, a great and a small.
You shall not have in your house differing measures, a great and a small.
You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.
For everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination unto the Lord your God.
